evidence.source: Wu Yuanyuan, Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Characters Civilization Research
evidence.field: §2.1.1, Shang numeral spellings; H.16189 and H.37453
evidence.text: The article reports that 三 is the only graph it found for the numeral three in Shang sources, citing oracle-bone corpus examples H.16189 and H.37453. It gives no precise date for either inscription. This supports an early numeral use, not a full chronology of the spoken word’s later senses.
evidence.kind: scholarly article reporting a corpus survey
evidence.title: 数词﹛三﹜的用字演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Wu Yuanyuan, Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Characters Civilization Research
evidence.text: The study reports 參 alongside 三 in Zhou sources, 品/晶 in Spring and Autumn and Warring States materials, and 三 and 參 in Qin-Han excavated texts. It excludes one transmitted Hanshu 叄 example from its Qin-Han count as possibly due to later substitution. These are alternative spellings of the numeral; the article does not present them as evidence that 三 was borrowed from another word.
evidence.kind: scholarly article reporting historical orthographic uses and a qualified textual assessment
evidence.title: 数词﹛三﹜的用字演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, International Computer Chinese Characters and Variant Forms Knowledgebase
evidence.field: 字形演變; bronze record 集成04261; Chu manuscripts; Small Seal; graph explanation
evidence.text: The page lists a bronze-script record 集成04261, Chu manuscript forms and a Small Seal form. It explains the three equal horizontal strokes as three equal counting rods representing three. This is the database’s paleographic interpretation; it does not establish that the earliest graph was devised by directly copying physical rods. The page also displays form images, but its rights notice reserves image and content rights, so its glyphs are not selected here as reusable assets.
evidence.title: 漢字「三」：字形演變

gaps: No original oracle-bone or bronze facsimile was independently inspected. The Shang numeral examples are reported by the corpus study without a precise reign or year.

The counting-rod explanation is the Academia Sinica page’s interpretation. Direct derivation of the earliest graph from physical rods is not established; the later Shuowen Heaven-Earth-humanity interpretation is a separate historical account.

The inspected sources document early numeral use and alternative numeral spellings, not a full dated chronology of semantic extensions of the spoken numeral. No chronology is inferred from a dictionary gloss list.

No sound component or whole-graph phonetic loan is proposed for 三. The supplied Baxter–Sagart possible influence from 四 concerns a spoken reconstruction, not graphic formation; the comparative Proto-Sino-Tibetan proposal was not independently assessed in this pass.

The Commons file page result supports a modern Liushutong-style vector redraw and public-domain declaration, but its page could not be opened interactively and the pixels were not inspected. Do not describe it as an artifact photograph or as an oracle-bone/bronze witness.
